title: In 1858 the Thames stank so badly that Parliament finally paid to fix London's sewers

cover.alt: A man in a top hat holds a lantern in a long brick sewer tunnel that curves away into the dark.

body: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames, which took London's sewage, smelled so foul that Parliament hung chemical-soaked canvas over its windows. Within weeks it passed an act to clean up the river, and the engineer **Joseph Bazalgette** built 82 miles of intercepting sewers that caught the sewage and carried it east, to be let out downstream on the ebb tide. The stink itself spread no disease; cholera travels in dirty water. When it struck London again in 1866 it killed 5,596 people, most of them in the East End, the one district his system did not yet reach. It was the city's last cholera epidemic.

slides.alt: A hot, hazy summer day on the Thames at Westminster. The river is brown and scummy; a boatman and a gentleman on the bank hold their noses. Behind them stands the Palace of Westminster, its clock tower still in scaffolding.
slides.caption: London, June 1858. On the 16th it reaches 94.5°F (34.7°C) in the shade at Greenwich, and the low, filthy Thames stinks.

slides.alt: Inside Parliament, a workman on a ladder hangs wet canvas over a tall Gothic window onto the river, a pail at its foot. Two members cover their noses with handkerchiefs.
slides.caption: At Parliament, canvas soaked in chloride of zinc and lime is hung over the windows that face the river.

slides.alt: A cut-away drawing of the city: drains run from each house down into a sewer, which slopes under the street and pours into the Thames. Arrows show the tide washing back and forth.
slides.caption: Why it stinks: London's sewers empty straight into the Thames, and the tide washes the filth up and down past the city.

slides.alt: The House of Commons: rows of members on green benches. Benjamin Disraeli, with black curls and a tuft of beard on his chin, stands at the table speaking.
slides.caption: 15 July: the Chancellor, Benjamin Disraeli, brings in a bill to clean up the river. It becomes law on 2 August, 18 days later.

bubbles.text: A Stygian pool, reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors.
bubbles.speaker: Benjamin Disraeli

slides.alt: Joseph Bazalgette, with a bald crown and dark side-whiskers, points at a large plan of London: the blue Thames winds across it, and red sewers run along both banks to two outfalls in the east.
slides.caption: The engineer Joseph Bazalgette has a plan: 82 miles of intercepting sewers to catch the old ones and carry it all east.

bubbles.text: We catch it before it reaches the river and send it far downstream.
bubbles.speaker: Joseph Bazalgette

slides.alt: In a deep timber-shored trench, bricklayers turn a brick arch over wooden centring. In the foreground Bazalgette, in a top hat, holds up a lantern.
slides.caption: Work starts in 1859. The system takes some 318 million bricks, and he builds it big enough for a growing city.

slides.alt: Inside the Crossness pumping station: painted iron columns in red, green and gold, a huge beam engine with its flywheel, and guests in top hats and bonnets.
slides.caption: 4 April 1865: the Prince of Wales opens the Crossness pumping station, whose great beam engines lift the sewage on its way out.

slides.alt: A cut-away of the Victoria Embankment: people stroll along the road on top; inside lie a round brick sewer and an underground railway with a train; a granite wall faces the river.
slides.caption: 1870: the Victoria Embankment opens, with a main sewer and an underground railway built inside it.

slides.question: Where did Bazalgette's sewers take London's sewage?
options: Downstream, out on the ebb tide
slides.explanation: They carried it east to outfalls at Beckton and Crossness and let it out on the ebb tide. Treating sewage came decades later.
